The Blunt scalyhead, Trematomus eulepidotus, is a benthic nototheniid endemic to the high-latitude waters of the Southern Ocean. Like many Antarctic notothenioids, this species exhibits a slow, deliberate life history shaped by the extreme thermal regime of its habitat. Field collections and laboratory rearing studies have provided quantitative insights into its growth and reproduction. Egg diameter averages approximately 2 mm, and from this, the calculated wet weight of a newly hatched larva is estimated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a minute size reflecting the limited yolk reserves typical of pelagic-spawning nototheniids. The incubation period for the developing embryo is highly dependent on temperature; at a constant 0 °C [T = 0 °C], the time from fertilisation to eclosion has been documented to be approximately 95 days [ab = approximately 95 days]. This protracted embryonic stage is consistent with the developmental rates observed in congeneric species such as Trematomus bernacchii, and represents an adaptive compromise between the need for adequate organogenesis and the constraints of a near-freezing thermal environment.

As juveniles transition into the sub-adult phase, body length and mass increase steadily, following a power-law relationship with body length. Reproductive maturation is reached at a comparatively modest size. Analyses of gonadal condition from trawl-caught specimens indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters]. Using the species-specific length-weight conversion, the corresponding wet weight at this life stage is calculated to be 116.5 grams [Wwp = 116.5 grams]. This relatively late maturity, occurring at roughly two-thirds of the maximum observed length, is a common feature among Antarctic fishes, likely an adaptive response to the strong seasonality of food supply in the Southern Ocean. Reaching this size requires several years of sustained feeding on benthic prey, primarily amphipods and polychaetes, before the fish can divert resources into gamete production. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is tightly linked to the brief austral summer phytoplankton bloom.

Full somatic growth is achieved only after many years. The ultimate total length recorded for this species, based on extensive survey data, is 34.5 centimeters [Li = 34.5 centimeters]. At this asymptotic size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight is estimated using the length-mass regression at 505.2 grams [Wwi = 505.2 grams]. Adult specimens approaching this size are relatively uncommon in trawl samples, suggesting that the species experiences considerable natural mortality before reaching its maximum dimensions. The ultimate body size places T. eulepidotus among the medium-sized nototheniids, somewhat larger than its congener T. bernacchii but substantially smaller than the colossal Dissostichus mawsoni. This size trajectory, combined with sustained cold temperatures, imposes a fundamental constraint on the species' capacity for population turnover and annual reproductive output.

Reproductive effort in T. eulepidotus is constrained by the cold, which slows metabolic processes and limits the rate at which energy can be mobilized for egg production. In the stable thermal conditions of McMurdo Sound, where water temperatures hover near -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C], the maximum daily rate of reproduction has been estimated. Adult females are capable of producing, on average, approximately 33 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 33 eggs per day] throughout a protracted spawning season, yielding a total annual fecundity that supports population persistence under challenging conditions. This fecundity estimate aligns with the relatively low energy availability in polar ecosystems, where a high per-event investment is traded off against a slower pace of life. The same thermal constraint that limits reproductive rate also governs somatic maintenance. Under the persistently cold conditions of -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species has been recorded at 19 years [am = 19 years], a longevity that is considerable for a teleost of this body size and which underscores a life-history strategy dominated by survival over rapid turnover.

Comparisons with other nototheniids highlight the conservative life-history strategy of T. eulepidotus. The 19-year maximum lifespan (19 years) [am = 19 years] documented at -0.9 °C [T = -0.9 °C] is notably longer than that of temperate perciforms of similar body mass, reflecting the profoundly retarded aging rates seen in polar ectotherms. This extreme longevity, combined with a delayed puberty at 22 cm [Lp = 22 cm] total length and a modest daily reproductive output of approximately 33 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 33 eggs per day], suggests that the species relies on high adult survival and iteroparity to buffer against sporadic recruitment failures. The very low initial wet weight of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] for a larva emerging from an incubation of 95 days [ab = 95 days] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C] exemplifies the high cost of development in the cold. Such life-history traits make the Blunt scalyhead vulnerable to environmental warming, as any increase in metabolic demand without a compensatory increase in food availability could erode the energy surplus necessary for reproduction and long-term somatic maintenance.
